articles.title: Scientists discover new Alzheimer’s drug that repairs DNA damage and reduces brain inflammation
articles.summary: Scientists have discovered that a drug originally developed for spinal cord injuries can tackle several key features of Alzheimer’s disease, including DNA damage and inflammation. Already tested for initial safety in humans, the experimental treatment could offer a faster path toward therapies that target the disease at its roots.
articles.content:
Scientists at King's College London have identified a promising new strategy for fighting Alzheimer's disease that could address several of the condition's damaging effects at the same time. Their research suggests that an experimental drug originally developed for spinal cord injuries may help repair damaged DNA, reduce inflammation, and target biological changes associated with the disease.

The drug, known as KCL-286, produced encouraging results in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. Unlike treatments that focus primarily on the buildup of toxic proteins in the brain, this approach targets additional processes that can begin long before the disease reaches its advanced stages.

One particularly promising advantage is that KCL-286 has already completed Phase 1 human safety and tolerability trials as part of its earlier development. This could significantly shorten the path toward further clinical testing, although its effectiveness against Alzheimer's in humans has not yet been established.

"KCL-286 is a first-in-class, orally bioavailable small molecule that has already successfully cleared Phase 1 human safety and tolerability trials. This will dramatically cut down the traditional multi-year timeline required for new drug development," commented Professor Jonathan Corcoran, Professor of Neuroscience at the Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology & Neuroscience at King's College London.

The drug is a small molecule that can be taken by mouth, making it potentially more convenient to administer than treatments that require injections or infusions.

Why Alzheimer's Disease Is So Difficult to Treat

Alzheimer's disease involves a complicated series of changes in the brain, making it particularly challenging to develop effective treatments. Two of its best-known features are the abnormal accumulation of proteins called amyloid-beta and tau.

Amyloid-beta can collect into sticky deposits between nerve cells, while abnormal tau proteins can form tangles inside them. These changes interfere with normal brain function and are associated with the progressive loss of neurons, the specialized cells responsible for transmitting information throughout the brain.

Much of the effort to develop Alzheimer's treatments has focused on these two proteins. Although medications that remove amyloid-beta have demonstrated modest but measurable clinical benefits, they do not fully address the many biological processes involved in the disease.

Researchers are increasingly investigating other changes that may contribute to Alzheimer's, including damage to DNA and inflammation in the brain. Both can appear early in the disease process, making them potentially valuable targets for treatments designed to slow its progression.

In the new study, KCL-286 helped repair breaks in DNA and reduce inflammation in mice with Alzheimer's-like disease. These findings suggest that targeting several harmful processes simultaneously could offer a broader approach than focusing on amyloid-beta or tau alone.

"Our findings demonstrate that KCL-286 not only targets DNA damage but also reduces inflammation, two processes that occur very early in Alzheimer's disease progression. This highlights its potential as a disease-modifying therapy rather than simply addressing symptoms," said Dr. Maria Goncalves, who project-managed the drug development.

How Vitamin A Pathways Could Help Fight Alzheimer's

The drug works by activating a particular protein involved in the retinoic acid pathway, a biological system associated with how the body processes and uses vitamin A.

Vitamin A is best known for supporting healthy vision, but it also plays important roles in cellular development, gene regulation, and nervous system function. Retinoic acid, a substance derived from vitamin A, helps control the activity of genes involved in several essential biological processes.

Earlier research found that disruptions in this pathway were associated with the formation of amyloid-beta deposits in the brains of rats. These deposits resemble a major pathological feature of Alzheimer's disease, suggesting that the pathway may be relevant to the condition.

KCL-286 activates a specific protein within this system, offering researchers a way to influence biological processes connected to brain health and cellular repair.

The drug had already demonstrated an ability to promote the repair of DNA double-strand breaks in earlier research involving neuropathic pain, a type of pain caused by damage or dysfunction in the nervous system.

That discovery led scientists to investigate whether the same mechanism might also help address DNA damage associated with Alzheimer's disease.

Repairing a Dangerous Type of DNA Damage

DNA contains the genetic instructions that cells need to function properly. Although cells have natural systems for repairing damaged DNA, some forms of damage are particularly serious.

One example is a DNA double-strand break, which occurs when both strands of the DNA molecule are severed. These breaks can disrupt normal cellular activity and threaten cell survival if they are not properly repaired.

"DNA double-strand breaks are like a rope snapping completely in two, rather than just fraying at the edges. We found that KCL-286 promotes repair of these breaks, allowing us to target a key feature of Alzheimer's disease," said Professor Corcoran.

The researchers had another reason to suspect that KCL-286 might be useful against Alzheimer's. Previous work by the same team at King's College London identified molecular pathways shared by acute spinal cord injury and Alzheimer's disease.

Because the two conditions involve some overlapping biological mechanisms, the scientists believed that a drug developed to address nervous system damage after spinal cord injury might also improve certain Alzheimer's-related changes in neurons.

Their new findings support that possibility, showing that KCL-286 can influence several cellular pathways involved in the disease.

A Promising New Direction for Alzheimer's Treatment

The results highlight a potentially important shift in Alzheimer's research. Rather than concentrating on one hallmark of the disease, scientists are exploring treatments that address several interconnected causes of brain damage.

KCL-286 is particularly interesting because it targets DNA damage and inflammation, two processes that can emerge early in Alzheimer's progression. Its previous human safety testing also provides a potential advantage over entirely new drug candidates that have not yet entered clinical development.

However, the Alzheimer's findings remain preclinical. Additional studies and human clinical trials will be necessary to determine whether the drug can safely slow disease progression or improve outcomes in patients.

Natasha Hill, one of the first authors on the paper, said: "To develop an effective treatment for Alzheimer's disease, we need to tackle multiple aspects of the disease. KCL-286 was able to target multiple disease-relevant cellular pathways, some of which are initiated very early in the disease course."
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant scientific discovery of a drug that targets multiple damaging processes in Alzheimer's disease, including DNA damage and inflammation, with promising preclinical results and prior human safety testing. This represents a meaningful potential breakthrough in treating a major public health challenge, with broad significance and detailed context.

articles.title: Scientists reverse liver cell aging and cut Alzheimer’s-linked protein in half
articles.summary: A surprising discovery suggests that rejuvenating the liver could help protect against Alzheimer’s disease and heart disease. USC researchers found that an experimental drug restored aging liver cells in rats, cutting levels of an Alzheimer’s-linked protein in half and bringing bad cholesterol down to youthful levels. The treatment also revived a previously unknown communication system that helps liver cells remove harmful substances from the bloodstream.
articles.content:
The liver may hold an unexpected key to fighting two of the most serious diseases associated with aging: Alzheimer's disease and heart disease. Scientists have discovered that restoring the function of aging liver cells can dramatically reduce harmful substances in the bloodstream, raising the possibility of treating diseases that affect organs far beyond the liver itself.

In a new study involving older rats, researchers at the Keck School of Medicine of USC found that an experimental drug called cinaciguat reversed important signs of aging in specialized liver cells. After just two weeks of treatment, levels of amyloid beta, a protein associated with Alzheimer's disease, dropped by half. Levels of LDL, commonly called bad cholesterol, also returned to those seen in younger animals.

The findings, published in the Journal of Biological Chemistry, also revealed a previously unknown way that liver cells communicate with one another. This discovery could help scientists develop treatments that restore the liver's ability to remove potentially harmful substances from the blood, possibly reducing the risk of Alzheimer's disease and atherosclerosis, a condition in which fatty deposits accumulate inside arteries.

Why the Liver Could Be Important for Alzheimer's

Although Alzheimer's primarily affects the brain, scientists are increasingly interested in how other organs might influence the disease. The liver plays a central role in filtering the blood and removing unwanted compounds, including substances that may contribute to disease when they accumulate.

The USC findings suggest that restoring this natural cleaning process could offer a different approach to preventing certain age-related illnesses. However, the results have so far been demonstrated only in rats, and additional studies are needed to establish whether the same benefits occur in humans.

"We need to do further translational work to see whether our findings might point to new therapies," said corresponding author Laurie DeLeve, MD, PhD, professor and vice chair for scientific affairs in the USC Department of Medicine. "We're hopeful, though, because the findings line up with a lot of epidemiological results showing age as a major risk factor for Alzheimer's and atherosclerosis, and liver damage as a risk factor for Alzheimer's."

Targeting the liver could be particularly valuable in Alzheimer's research, where efforts to develop treatments acting directly in the brain have faced an estimated 98% failure rate in clinical trials. One major obstacle is the blood-brain barrier, a protective system that limits which substances can enter the brain from the bloodstream. While this barrier helps shield the brain from harmful compounds, it also makes delivering certain medications extremely difficult.

"If we're right that the liver is impactful, what do we do about that?" said first author Sam de Leve, MA, a USC lab technician and child of Laurie DeLeve. "Rather than trying to get a drug through the blood-brain barrier, which is obnoxiously difficult, we could direct drugs to the liver, an organ where there might be more therapeutic impact and certainly an easier job of drug delivery."

Scientists Restore the Aging Liver's Natural Filters

To understand how liver aging affects the bloodstream, the researchers focused on a relatively understudied group of cells known as liver sinusoidal endothelial cells (LSECs).

These cells form the lining of tiny blood vessels inside the liver. Unlike most blood vessel walls, they contain numerous microscopic openings that function somewhat like the holes in a sieve. These openings allow larger molecules circulating in the blood to reach neighboring cells called hepatocytes, which carry out much of the liver's work processing and removing substances from the body.

As the liver ages, the openings in LSECs gradually become smaller or disappear. This makes it harder for certain large molecules to reach the cells responsible for clearing them, allowing more of these substances to remain in circulation.

One substance affected by this change is amyloid beta. This protein is especially important in Alzheimer's research because it can accumulate in the brain and form plaques, one of the disease's defining features.

Previous observations showed that the liver becomes less effective at removing amyloid beta as it ages. The researchers suspected that the gradual closing of the openings in LSECs might help explain why more of the protein remains in the bloodstream of older animals.

To investigate, they administered cinaciguat to aged rats for two weeks. They then compared the treated animals with two untreated groups, one consisting of older rats and the other of younger rats.

The results were striking. Cinaciguat restored the structure and function of the aging LSECs, reopening their microscopic pores and improving their ability to help clear substances from the blood. Amyloid beta concentrations fell by approximately 50%, reaching levels comparable to those in young rats. The untreated older animals showed no similar improvement.

An Unexpected Drop in Bad Cholesterol

The researchers also measured low-density lipoproteins (LDL), often referred to as "bad" cholesterol because elevated levels contribute to fatty deposits inside arteries. Over time, these deposits can restrict blood flow and increase the risk of heart disease.

Initially, LDL was included as a comparison measure rather than a substance expected to respond to treatment. Unlike larger molecules, LDL particles are small enough to leave the bloodstream without passing through the microscopic openings in LSECs. The scientists therefore expected cinaciguat to have little or no effect on LDL levels.

Instead, they discovered that LDL concentrations in treated older rats also fell to levels observed in young animals.

"We said, 'Wait, why did that go down? Clearly, there's more to this story,'" Sam de Leve said.

The unexpected finding suggested that the drug was doing more than simply reopening the liver's aging filters. It appeared to be restoring another important aspect of liver function.

Because previous research had shown that hepatocytes function better when LSECs are present, the team began examining how these two types of cells communicate.

Their investigation uncovered a previously unknown sequence of biochemical signals that helps coordinate the liver's ability to remove substances from the bloodstream.

A Hidden Communication Pathway Between Liver Cells

The researchers found that cinaciguat activates an enzyme called soluble guanylate cyclase inside LSECs. This triggers the cells to release a growth factor known as HB-EGF, which sends a signal to nearby hepatocytes.

In response, hepatocytes alter their surfaces in ways that allow them to capture more LDL and amyloid beta from the blood. This helps explain why the treatment reduced both substances, even though they do not rely on the same filtering mechanism.

Normally, aging interferes with the ability of LSECs to release HB-EGF. Cinaciguat restored this signaling process, allowing the liver cells to communicate more effectively and supporting the removal of substances that otherwise tend to accumulate with age.

The discovery identifies a potential new target for future drugs. Rather than focusing exclusively on the physical openings in LSECs, researchers may be able to develop therapies that restore the chemical signals responsible for helping the liver work efficiently.

Could Liver Rejuvenation Help Prevent Alzheimer's and Heart Disease?

According to the researchers, this is the first study to demonstrate that a drug can fully restore the structure and function of aging LSECs, including their ability to support the clearance of substances from the bloodstream.

It is also the first to show that a treatment directed at the liver can bring age-related elevations in circulating amyloid beta and LDL back to youthful levels.

These findings raise the possibility that cinaciguat, similar medications, or treatments targeting HB-EGF could eventually be used to counteract certain effects of liver aging. If those changes translate into meaningful protection against disease, they could provide new strategies for preventing Alzheimer's and cardiovascular problems.

For now, however, the findings represent an early step. Lowering amyloid beta in the bloodstream does not necessarily mean that amyloid plaques in the brain will decrease or that Alzheimer's disease can be prevented.

The researchers plan to continue studying cinaciguat in rats to determine whether its effects on amyloid beta actually translate into measurable protection against Alzheimer's disease.

They also hope the findings will encourage scientists studying other conditions, particularly atherosclerosis, to investigate how restoring liver function might influence disease development.

"We hope that people who are in fields like atherosclerosis research read this, and want to grab the idea for themselves," Sam de Leve said. "There are six different ways someone could go with this, and we can't do them all. So please, scoop us. We'd love it."

Study Authors and Funding

Additional researchers involved in the study include Xiangdong Wang, Helia Alavifard and Lily Dara, all affiliated with the Keck School of Medicine of USC.

The research received federal funding from the National Institutes of Health [R56AG071480, 5R01DK100580].

articles.title: Experts say high blood pressure guidelines are missing half the equation
articles.summary: Scientists are calling for a major rethink of how we manage high blood pressure, suggesting that eating more potassium could be just as important as cutting back on salt. A new report finds that combining increased potassium intake with reduced sodium consumption may offer greater benefits for blood pressure control than sodium reduction alone.
articles.content:
For decades, one of the most common recommendations for lowering high blood pressure has been simple: eat less salt. But a new scientific report suggests that this advice may be missing an equally important part of the equation.

Researchers say that increasing potassium intake, rather than focusing only on reducing sodium, could lead to better blood pressure control. By addressing both nutrients together, this approach could strengthen efforts to prevent hypertension and reduce the risk of serious cardiovascular problems.

The potential impact is enormous. High blood pressure, also known as hypertension, affects more than 1.28 billion adults worldwide and is a major risk factor for cardiovascular disease, including heart attacks and strokes. Although public health recommendations have traditionally emphasized cutting sodium, researchers now argue that getting enough potassium deserves just as much attention.

Why Potassium Matters for Blood Pressure

Sodium and potassium are essential minerals that help regulate fluid balance, nerve signaling, and muscle function. Both also influence blood pressure, but they affect the body in different ways.

Eating too much sodium can cause the body to retain additional fluid, increasing the pressure inside blood vessels. Potassium helps counter some of sodium's effects by supporting the kidneys in removing excess sodium through urine. It also contributes to the normal functioning of blood vessel walls, which plays an important role in maintaining healthy blood pressure.

In a new report, physicians and health experts argue that dietary recommendations should address these two minerals together. Rather than treating sodium reduction as the primary solution, they propose combining it with greater potassium consumption to achieve stronger results.

"It is time to view dietary interventions holistically because food components interact and physiology is integrative across systems," said Naomi Fukagawa, M.D. Ph.D., professor of medicine emerita at the Robert Larner, M.D. College of Medicine at the University of Vermont and first author on the report. "Growing evidence shows that increasing dietary potassium as well as reducing sodium intake work together to better manage hypertension."

A Major Rethink of Blood Pressure Guidelines

The report, published in the peer-reviewed American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, was supported by the IAFNS Sodium in Food and Health Implications Committee.

The researchers examined the scientific evidence underlying current sodium and potassium recommendations, along with practical ways to reduce sodium consumption and increase potassium intake. They also explored the obstacles to implementing these changes and identified areas where additional research and updated public health policies could help improve outcomes.

One of the central concerns is that many people consume too much sodium while getting nowhere near enough potassium. Both dietary patterns can contribute to elevated blood pressure, making them important targets for prevention and treatment.

Despite widespread efforts to encourage people to limit salt, average sodium consumption continues to exceed recommended levels. Meanwhile, potassium intake remains "far below optimal levels in both developed and developing nations," according to the authors.

This imbalance suggests that focusing primarily on what people should eat less of may be overlooking an important opportunity to improve cardiovascular health by encouraging them to consume more of a beneficial nutrient.

How to Get More Potassium in Your Diet

Potassium is naturally present in many familiar foods, including fruits, vegetables, legumes, and dairy products. Bananas, potatoes, beans, leafy greens, and yogurt are examples of foods that can help increase potassium intake.

Another possibility is replacing some sodium chloride, the main ingredient in ordinary table salt, with potassium salts. These substitutes can help reduce sodium while simultaneously increasing potassium, potentially addressing both dietary goals at once.

However, creating these products presents challenges for food manufacturers. Adding too much potassium salt can produce an unpleasant metallic taste, limiting how much can be used without affecting flavor. Manufacturers must therefore find a balance that improves nutritional content while keeping foods appealing to consumers.

Increasing potassium is also not appropriate for everyone. People with kidney disease or those taking certain medications may have difficulty regulating potassium levels, so potassium supplements and potassium-based salt substitutes should be used with medical guidance when these concerns apply.

A New Strategy for Fighting High Blood Pressure

The researchers emphasize that reducing sodium remains essential. Their proposal is not to abandon existing advice, but to expand it by recognizing that potassium intake is another major factor in blood pressure regulation.

The authors conclude that "dietary sodium reduction is a foundational strategy for hypertension prevention and management. However, new evidence supports a broadening of the current approach that focuses solely on sodium reduction and provides equal emphasis on increasing potassium intake."

articles.title: We are finally pinning down what makes dyslexic brains different
articles.summary: Humans never evolved to read and write, and around 10 per cent of us are dyslexic. Now, we are uncovering the pathways underlying the condition, opening up new ways to support people who struggle to read
articles.content:
Humans never evolved to read and write, and around 10 per cent of us are dyslexic. Now, we are uncovering the pathways underlying the condition, opening up new ways to support people who struggle to read

Owen Gildersleeve

I used to be stupid. It was a long time ago and I was very young – too young to question teachers who said I was a bit dim. Besides, wasn’t there proof? I had been slow to learn to read, my spelling was atrocious and my aptitude for climbing trees wasn’t fooling anyone. So, I believed them. Then, aged 7, everything changed. For the first time, I had a teacher who saw beyond my literary ineptitude. She told me I was smart – and, suddenly, I was. Thank you, Mrs Kennedy!

That was more than 50 years ago. Back then, dyslexia already had a long history, but news of it hadn’t reached the classroom – at least none I found myself in. Children like me usually weren’t given a diagnosis or special help. Far from it. At the convent school I attended next, spelling tests were a ritual humiliation, where the nuns lined us up against a wall in the order of our results and shamed those who failed to perform.

Things have changed since then. Teachers are fully aware of dyslexia. Children with this, the most common of learning disabilities, are no longer labelled “stupid” or “lazy”. Huge volumes of research have been published. Yet, fierce disagreements have also raged about what causes dyslexia and how best to diagnose and treat it.

Advertisement

Now, finally, we are pinning down what makes dyslexic brains different. We may even have found the key neural pathway that drives the condition. Better yet, this research is pointing to novel, practical and fairer ways to help all children who struggle to read.

Humans invented writing around 5000 years ago – far too recently to have evolved an adaptation for deciphering the written word. Besides, for most of our history, the vast majority of humanity has been illiterate. So, when we learn to read, our brains must co-opt areas specialised for other functions. That this isn’t straightforward for everyone has long been recognised. The word dyslexia (from the Greek for “disordered words”) was coined in 1883 to describe a curious condition in which experiencing a stroke had left a person unable to read or spell. But, within a few years, it was being used for a far larger group – children who find it hard to acquire these skills.

The Epic of Gilgamesh, one of the oldest surviving literary works, is over 4000 years old. But in evolutionary terms, writing is a very recent invention Album/Alamy

Developmental dyslexia is often described as a significant and persistent difficulty with reading and spelling. Traditionally, the definition has also included the idea that these difficulties are unexpected given the child’s other cognitive abilities – although the recently updated definition issued by the International Dyslexia Association has finally dropped this controversial “discrepancy” idea. We know that both genes and environment play a role, that dyslexia is a spectrum and that it can manifest in different ways, such as spelling difficulties (a particular problem in alphabetic language systems), slow reading and writing speeds, or both.

All this makes its prevalence hard to quantify. Most estimates put it at around 10 per cent of people globally; some say twice that. What’s more certain is that dyslexia is a universal human condition found in all languages and writing systems.

Reading is cognitively complicated. It entails three key components: understanding how sounds relate to squiggles on a page (phonology); mastering the patterns of written words and the rules of spelling (orthography); and making sense of what you see (semantics). To do this, your brain recruits networks evolved to process vision and speech and links them into a new “reading circuit”. This is located primarily in the brain’s left hemisphere and also comprises three main components. The occipitotemporal region, located low in the back of the brain, instantly recognises those squiggles as words, hence its common name: the “visual word form area”. Word shapes are matched to sounds in the temporoparietal junction, above and behind your left ear. And further forward, the inferior frontal gyrus (Broca’s area) handles speech production and meaning.

A widespread network of brain pathways is active during reading, reflecting the cognitive complexity involved Brian A. Wandell; Rosemary K. Le

The underlying circuitry is the same, regardless of the language or script – even for writing systems that don’t look anything alike, such as those for English and Chinese.

Clearly, there is a lot that can go wrong, not just in the reading circuit, but in other aspects of reading such as attention, memory, processing speed, logical thinking and knowledge of vocabulary. So perhaps it shouldn’t surprise us that, over the years, researchers have come up with a wide range of ideas to explain the condition.

One of the most prominent is the phonological deficit theory, which asserts that the problem lies in poor awareness of speech sounds and difficulty relating these to written symbols. “This is now considered to be a primary deficit,” says Maggie Snowling, a psychologist at the University of Oxford who has long been a proponent of the idea. Phonological deficit and a second problem known as rapid automatised naming (RAN) – slowness in identifying letters, numbers and even pictures – constitute the “double-deficit hypothesis”.

Then there are explanations that focus on the brain itself. Temporal processing theory, for instance, points to an underlying problem of timing in the way the auditory system processes sounds, which has profound knock-on effects for reading and writing. The magnocellular hypothesis, in contrast, places an emphasis on visual attention. It stems from findings that magnocellular neurons, which process fast-moving visual information, are less active and less numerous in people with dyslexia.

In short, decades of research have generated plenty of ideas, but not much consensus. A major roadblock has been that studies were small and not easily compared. This is now being addressed thanks to the availability of large-scale longitudinal datasets and improved methods. That may not sound dramatic, but it has been a game changer.

Take genetics. Clearly, dyslexia runs in families: I have my father to thank for mine. “The heritability you see in twin studies is about 70 per cent,” says Michelle Luciano, who studies behavioural genetics at the University of Edinburgh in the UK. That’s massive – but comes with a big caveat. “It’s not just the genes; it’s the gene-environment correlation that’s really important,” says Snowling. The idea is that factors such as low birth weight and whether literacy is encouraged at home play a key part in shaping the chances of developing dyslexia in those with a genetic susceptibility.

There is also no single dyslexia gene – many tiny genetic changes interact to generate the condition in all its guises. And tracking them down is fiendishly difficult. Traditional methods of genetic analysis identified several “candidate” genes that people with dyslexia appear to share. Now, geneticists can scan full genomes looking for variants linked with complex traits – and do this at scale. The first such genome-wide association study (GWAS) on dyslexia was published in 2022.

Using information from the 23andMe genetic database, a team led by Luciano analysed the genomes of 51,800 people with a dyslexia diagnosis and over 1 million controls. This revealed something surprising about those previously identified candidate genes. “A lot of these actually haven’t turned out to be that important,” says Luciano. The analysis did, however, identify 42 genetic variants linked with a risk of dyslexia. “Many of these genes had already been reported as being associated with either general cognitive ability or educational attainment,” she says. “But we also found several novel ones that may be more specific to language and reading.”

The study highlights the genetic complexity of dyslexia. It also confirms observed links with some neurodevelopmental conditions such as ADHD – but not others. “For autism, for instance, we found no genetic overlap,” says Luciano. She and her colleagues have since worked on an even larger dataset of more than 1.2 million people, identifying a further 13 genes related to dyslexia that implicate early brain developmental processes in the biological underpinning of reading. “Genetic studies give us a possibility to bridge the gap between cognitive theories and neuroscience,” she says.

In fact, these genetic findings have already provided a springboard for a giant leap in revealing the neuroanatomy of dyslexia. A team led by Clyde Francks at the Max Planck Institute for Psycholinguistics in Nijmegen, the Netherlands, used them to calculate the genetic predisposition to dyslexia of 35,231 people in the UK Biobank database. They then identified brain regions that differed in people whose genes put them at risk of dyslexia. (I must now declare an interest: I have been in the UK Biobank project from the start, done all the tests and had my genome sequenced and my brain scanned, so one of those 35,231 people is me.)

Francks and his colleagues found that the genetic risk of dyslexia was associated with widespread reduction in brain volume compared with people not at genetic risk, especially in language-related and motor areas. (Yikes!) Again, there were correlations with ADHD and other neurodevelopmental conditions – although reductions in the motor cortex were specifically linked with dyslexia. That might seem strange, but motor control could affect reading in a variety of ways, says Francks. “For example, infants with better motor skills might be able to learn language-related skills more quickly through better coordination when producing speech sounds, pointing to track letters and words or keeping time during chants and songs.”

Meanwhile, earlier this year, another impressive large-scale study finally nailed a long-standing debate in the field over the contribution of visual difficulties, not just phonological ones, to reading problems. “We and others have long held the view that dyslexia is quite heterogenous, and phonological problems are only one part of the story,” says Jason Yeatman, who specialises in the neurobiology of reading at Stanford University.

Around one in ten children have dyslexia, and early intervention is crucial to help struggling readers Guerilla/Getty Images

He and his colleagues carried out tests on 400 children in kindergarten and first grade (typically aged 5-7) at California schools, measuring how quickly they processed visual information such as identifying the direction of dots moving on a computer screen. This revealed that around 15 per cent of the children had problems with visual-spatial attention, and these were associated with reading difficulties a year later. “These kids aren’t picked up by any of the conventional screening processes,” says Yeatman. What’s more, the research identified a hidden subgroup whose weak visual processing was masked by strong phonological skills.

But for many people with dyslexia, the primary problem is with phonology and, over the years, researchers have pinpointed a key neurological mechanism underlying these difficulties. It boils down to the way the brain processes the rhythm patterns of speech, in particular the rates of change in loudness that mark the beginning of syllables – a cue that the brain uses to make sense of the stream of information it receives by chunking it into meaningful units. This is the basis of the temporal sampling theory devised by Usha Goswami at the University of Cambridge, which combines phonology with what is happening in the brain.

Neurons in the brain fire automatically in response to these sounds, which can be measured using EEG to visualise the brainwaves in the auditory cortex – even in infants who are just learning to speak. “You can think of word representations in the brain almost like auditory objects, like 3D mountains,” says Goswami. However, she and her colleagues have found that children with dyslexia have a subtle mismatch between speech sounds and these mental representations due to problems discerning rhythm and pitch, especially at low frequencies.

This doesn’t cause obvious issues with speech, but can have a profound impact on reading and writing, because these skills utilise speech-processing pathways to decode written words. “This really only hits when a child is learning to read,” says Goswami. “The whole shape of the mountain range will be a bit different, but they’re trying to learn to read and spell in a system made for children with another type of mountain range.”

For instance, a 2024 study by Goswami and her colleagues of more than 100 English-speaking children in Australia and the UK used EEG to measure their brain responses to speech, and found that issues with temporal sampling were strongly associated with dyslexia. What’s more, this technique could be used as the basis of a ‘classifier’ tool to identify children with the condition. “If we randomly select one child with dyslexia and one without dyslexia, the classifier has a 77 per cent chance of correctly identifying which child is more likely to have dyslexia, based on their brain responses to speech,” says auditory neuroscientist Mahmoud Keshavarzi at the University of Cambridge.

Indeed, Goswami thinks that difficulties with temporal sampling are the primary cause of dyslexia, and that the other problems associated with the condition arise during a child’s development. However, other researchers think that the condition is too heterogeneous to be driven by a single underlying factor. “The more recently accepted understanding is that dyslexia is a consequence of multiple biological and environmental risk factors,” says Julian Elliott at Durham University, UK, who researches dyslexia in children.

Still, there is clear evidence that boosting the ability of young children to process rhythms can improve their language skills – as demonstrated in a study by Goswami and her colleagues involving 120 children under the age of 11, which added activities such as drumming, chanting and marching to a beat into their classrooms. “These all help stamp in the rhythmic patterns which are so fundamental,” she says.

The team is also developing technologies specifically to help those with dyslexia. “We’ve found a neural characteristic called the theta-delta ratio, which is too high in children with dyslexia when they’re listening to natural speech,” says Goswami. One intervention allows children to visualise what is happening in their brain while listening to a story, via the movement of a little spaceship on a screen. “When they’re keeping the spaceship up, it means they’ve reduced their theta-delta ratio,” she says. This feedback leads to improvements in phonology and reading.

She isn’t alone in believing we can do more to help children who struggle with reading and spelling. Decades of tinkering make it clear that the key is a focus on phonics – specifically, training on phonemes, letters and single-sound associations, says Snowling. “But it’s also not everything,” says Yeatman. In addition, young readers require help tailored to their particular needs. For those with visual-processing problems, there is no reliable evidence that coloured lenses or special fonts work. But Yeatman’s team has found that this subset of children read faster when the spacing between letters is increased. He also thinks there is potential to train the visual system to work better through specially designed computer games. “This area is ripe for investigation,” he says.

Perhaps the biggest thing we can do is identify dyslexia early, as evidence shows that intensive interventions have significant effects on struggling readers, with the greatest influence if these are implemented in a child’s early school years. “I think it’s incredibly important,” says Snowling.

Another much-debated area is the best way to test for dyslexia. Assessments typically entail detailed tests, including whether there was a discrepancy between general level of cognitive ability and reading and writing attainment. However, the updated guidelines issued by the International Dyslexia Association have dropped this criterion, not least because it is biased against children from lower socioeconomic groups and those learning to read in a second language.

Elliott thinks there is further to go. For years he has been arguing that the terms “dyslexia” be replaced by “reading disability”, so that all children who need help get it. “There are no clear criteria that would enable an assessor to make a determination between a poor reader who gets a dyslexia diagnosis and one who doesn’t,” he says. “Neither is there any intervention suitable for a diagnosed reader that is not equally valuable for any other struggling reader.” His view is controversial, but perhaps that’s not surprising. “It threatens vested interests – a dyslexia industry that is worth billions of dollars,” he says.

There are undoubtedly still problems, but progress is being made. “I’m an optimist,” says Yeatman. Me, too. After all, my (admittedly mild) dyslexia hasn’t held me back as a journalist. Today, I have my spellchecker, and eagle-eyed subeditors to pick me up on more subtle slips like “wonton destruction”, which I once used in a quote from an ecologist (and, yes, he was Chinese). But I do think there is still a stigma associated with dyslexia. Otherwise, why would 85 per cent of people diagnosed with the condition not reveal this to their employer?

Times have changed, and so should attitudes. So, I’m admitting it here for the first time in my career: My name is Kate Douglas, and I am dyslexic.
